chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Hasan ibn Ribat from Abu Sara from Hind al-Sarrag who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), 'May Allah improve you, what do you say? I used to carry weapons to the people of Sham and sell them to them. When Allah made this matter clear to me, I felt constrained by that and said, 'I will not carry to the enemies of Allah.' He said to me, 'Carry to them, for indeed Allah, Exalted and Glorious, repels through them our enemy and your enemy, meaning the Romans. So when war is between us, whoever carries to our enemy weapons with which they will seek assistance against us, he is mushrik (polytheist/idolater).'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling weapons to non-Shia Muslims during peace and war?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the nuanced Shia jurisprudence of *al-mubah* (permissible) versus *al-muharram* (prohibited) based on the political context of the seller. Imam al-Sadiq distinguishes between selling arms to the Romans during peace, where they serve as a buffer against the Imams' enemies, and selling during war, where aiding them constitutes *mushriq* (associating with the enemy against the faithful). This highlights the strategic flexibility in commercial transactions within the framework of *ghaybah* and early Islamic geopolitics.
